document.title: Limited Protest of American Municipal Power, Inc. to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s proposal filed on 08/13/2026
document.group: PJM Large Load definition, Registry and Interim Resource Adequacy Service

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
Docket No. ER26-3515-000 
LIMITED PROTEST OF 
AMERICAN MUNICIPAL POWER, INC. 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy 
Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”),1 American Municipal Power, Inc. 
(“AMP”) submits this limited protest of the August 13, 2026 filing by PJM Interconnection, 
L.L.C. (“PJM”) in the above-captioned docket,2 in which PJM proposes revisions to its 
Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and Reliability Assurance Agreement Among 
Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) to establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”). 
AMP submits this limited protest to express concerns with PJM’s proposal for accrediting 
Bring Your Own New Capacity (“BYONC”), which fails to properly account for changes in 
accredited capacity values over time. 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
PJM is facing an enormous influx of new data center load, which threatens to 
exacerbate the region’s capacity shortfall and impose billions of dollars in additional costs 
on existing native load customers. It is imperative that PJM have the tools to 
accommodate these new loads while ensuring reliability and affordability for current 
customers. Consistent with the Ratepayer Protection Pledge,3 and longstanding cost

Filing”).

2 
causation principles, existing native load customers should not be required to shoulder 
the costs or reliability risks attributable to serving these new large loads. The IRAS 
proposal – aside from the concerns discussed below – appears to be a reasonable 
response to the challenges presented by new large loads. 
IRAS is “a new supplemental capacity product through which New Large Loads 
provide a load reduction service that is a tool available to PJM to manage resource 
adequacy shortfalls that would otherwise drive shedding of native loads.”4 New Large 
Loads that are not supported either by capacity from PJM’s proposed Reliability Backstop 
Procurement (“RBP”),5 or by capacity that qualifies as BYONC would be eligible to provide 
IRAS (“Eligible New Large Loads”).6 Under the IRAS proposal, in Delivery Years where 
auctions under PJM’s Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) construct fail to procure sufficient 
capacity to meet reliability requirements, “each Electric Distributor zone/area may be 
4  PJM Filing, Transmittal Letter at 22. The PJM Filing proposes to establish “Large Load” and “New Large 
Load” as new defined terms. See id. at 5. Large Load is defined as “end-use customer(s) load that has 
a cumulative peak load of 50 megawatts or greater at a single electrical site behind one or more points 
of interconnection, where for configurations involving multiple affiliated load facilities or multiple points 
of interconnection with affiliated load facilities behind them, all affiliated load facilities within a one-mile 
radius will be considered a single electrical site as further described in the PJM Manuals.” PJM Filing, 
Attachment A, proposed RAA, Art. 1 - Definitions. New Large Load is defined as: 
[E]nd-use customer load that is either (a) a Large Load that goes into service after June 1, 
2027, or (b) incremental load in-service after June 1, 2027, that increases the existing end-
use customer load at a single electrical site that, prior to such incremental load, did not 
previously meet the definition of Large Load. However, to the extent three consecutive 
Delivery Years meet the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii), then 
New Large Load shall mean end-use customer load that is either (a) a Large Load that 
goes into service after June 1 of the first Delivery Year for which the requirements of Tariff, 
Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii) are not met or (b) incremental load in-service after June 
1 of the first Delivery Year for which the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section 
IV(b)(iii) are not met that increases the existing end-use customer load at a single electrical 
site that, prior to such incremental load, did not previously meet the definition of Large 
Load. 
PJM Filing, Attachment A, proposed Tariff – Definitions – L-M-N.  
5
See PJM, Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy Concerns Stemming from 
Large Loads, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 (July 31, 2026). 
6
See, e.g., PJM Filing, Transmittal Letter at 69.

3 
directed by PJM dispatchers to reduce load up to the [megawatt] quantity of capacity 
attributable to Eligible New Large Loads in that zone/area.”7
PJM proposes numerous other Tariff and RAA revisions in support of the IRAS 
framework, including implementation of a Large Load Registry database, and 
establishment of BYONC as a new category of capacity that would “allow New Large 
Loads to remove themselves—in whole or in part—from the [megawatts] eligible for IRAS 
where such loads bring new capacity to the PJM Region.”8 Further, beginning with the 
2029/2030 Delivery Year, “PJM will exclude from the demand curve (i.e., the [Variable 
Resource Requirement] Curve used in RPM Auctions) the [megawatts] of New Large 
Loads that have not entered into BYONC arrangements” or do not have any associated 
RBP capacity.9
AMP actively participated in the Critical Issue Fast Path (“CIFP”) process that 
informed the development of the IRAS framework.10 During that process, AMP endorsed 
– and continues to endorse – many of the core features of PJM’s IRAS proposal, including 
the Large Load Registry, offsetting IRAS obligations with BYONC, preserving retail 
regulatory authority over the determination of the end use loads ultimately subject to 
IRAS, and the exclusion of unhedged New Large Loads from the Variable Resource 
Requirement Curve. In general, the PJM Filing proposes a reasonable framework to 
“connect and manage” new large loads in the PJM region. 
7
Id. at 6. PJM would implement IRAS “prior to calling on Pre-Emergency Load Management, placing 
IRAS appropriately at the beginning of PJM’s actions in the event of NERC Energy Emergency Alert 
Level 1.” Id. at 22; see also id. at 78-80. 
8
Id. at 50. 
9
Id. at 109. 
10 See id. at 15-17.

4 
There is at least one aspect of the PJM Filing, however, that the Commission 
should direct PJM to revise, in accordance with PJM’s advance consent to modifications 
that are consistent with its overarching objectives.11 The Commission should not accept 
PJM’s proposal to fix the level of BYONC for a generation or storage resource at the 
resource’s accredited capacity in the first year it is in an arrangement with a New Large 
Load.12 PJM’s proposal to fix BYONC at the first-year accreditation level risks over-
crediting New Large Loads for BYONC given PJM’s projections that the effective load 
carrying capability (“ELCC”) of certain resource classes (particularly storage resources) 
will decline significantly over the next decade. In addition, the PJM Filing does not 
adequately explain how its proposed treatment of BYONC in RPM capacity auctions will 
result in just and reasonable outcomes in light of projected ELCC changes over time. To 
address these concerns, PJM should be required to revise its proposal to better account 
for projected ELCC declines in resources supporting BYONC. 
II. 
LIMITED PROTEST 
A. 
PJM’s proposal to fix the Accredited UCAP of BYONC without 
accounting for declining ELCC could understate the need for IRAS. 
Under the IRAS framework, capacity that qualifies as BYONC would offset the 
amount of New Large Load eligible (i.e., required) to provide IRAS.13 In setting the level 
of this BYONC offset, PJM explains that “[f]or BYONC supported by any resource type 
(generation, storage, and demand-side), the Accredited UCAP of the BYONC ‘shall be 
the Accredited UCAP for the RPM Auction in which the BYONC cleared for the initial 
11 Id. at 121-25. 
12 See id. at 65-66. 
13 See generally, id. at 50-66.

5 
Delivery Year the BYONC is in an arrangement with the New Large Load.’”14 In other 
words, the Accredited UCAP of a resource supporting BYONC would be fixed based on 
the resource’s ELCC in the first Delivery Year that it is supporting New Large Load. 
The core problem with setting BYONC’s Accredited UCAP based on a single year 
snapshot is that ELCC is not expected to remain static for every resource category. The 
ELCCs of storage resources, in particular, are projected to decline significantly over the 
next decade, as shown by PJM’s recently posted preliminary ELCC Class Ratings for 
Delivery Years 2028/29 – 2042/43.15
Under PJM’s proposal, if a 200 MW New Large Load (after accounting for the 
Forecast Pool Requirement), comes online in 2029 and brings 200 MW UCAP of BYONC 
supported by four-hour Capacity Storage Resources for that year, then the load will have 
no IRAS responsibility in all future years. But PJM’s own projections indicate that by 
2031/2032, that storage resource would be accredited with only 119 MW of UCAP.16
14 Id. at 66 (quoting Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, sections VII(i)(i)-(ii)). More specifically, the level of 
the BYONC offset would be set using the Installed Capacity (“ICAP”) equivalent of this Accredited UCAP 
value. Id. at 65-66. 
15  Available at: https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/cifp-rbp/postings/preliminary-
elcc-class-ratings-for-period-dy28-dy42.pdf. 
16  A four-hour battery resource with capacity of 350 megawatts (MW) UCAP could be expected to provide 
200 MW of Accredited UCAP in the 2029/2030 Delivery Year based on the projected ELCC of 57 
percent. The same 350 MW resource would be expected to provide 119 MW of Accredited UCAP at the 
projected 2031/2032 ELCC of 34 percent.

6 
Giving New Large Load “credit” for Accredited UCAP of BYONC that exceeds the 
actual ELCC-measured Delivery Year capacity value of the resources supporting the 
BYONC raises reliability concerns under PJM’s IRAS proposal. The portion of a New 
Large Load that exceeds the ELCC-measured UCAP of a supporting BYONC resource 
is effectively the same as unhedged, Eligible New Large Load, but without the 
corresponding IRAS load curtailment obligation. PJM could be forced to implement 
emergency procedures driven by such unhedged New Large Loads, with the adverse 
reliability consequences falling broadly on native load customers and those New Large 
Loads that brought sufficient BYONC, in contravention of PJM’s objectives. 
While PJM projects most resource classes to have relatively stable ELCCs over 
the next decade (see the table above), the significant ELCC declines predicted for certain 
resource classes (particularly storage) highlight the need to address potential UCAP 
declines for all resources in the IRAS framework. Otherwise, PJM could understate the 
amount of New Large Load that should be considered Eligible New Large Load obligated 
to provide IRAS.17
B. 
PJM has not established that the proposed treatment of BYONC in the 
Base Residual Auction (“BRA”) will result in just and reasonable, and 
not unduly discriminatory rates. 
BYONC would be required to participate as a price taker in RPM auctions for ten 
consecutive Delivery Years “to ensure that BYONC clear the auction and obtain a 
17  Notably, PJM proposes to require Demand and DER Capacity Aggregation Resources to demonstrate 
their Accredited UCAP values “each year for a 10-year period using the Demand Response or DER 
Capacity Aggregation Resources installed capacity for the first Delivery Year after the BYONC is in an 
arrangement with the New Large Load.” PJM Filing, Transmittal Letter at 66 (quoting proposed Tariff, 
Attachment DD-4, section VII(i)(ii) (quotation marks omitted)). No similar requirement applies to 
generation or storage resources.

7 
capacity commitment.”18 Similarly, New Large Loads with BYONC arrangements would 
be reflected in the Variable Resource Requirement Curve.19 While it is reasonable to 
require BYONC to be offered in RPM auctions (and to be offered as a price-taker), PJM’s 
proposal lacks necessary clarity regarding how resources supporting BYONC will be 
accredited for BRA purposes, and how the PJM Filing will result in just and reasonable, 
and not unduly discriminatory outcomes in those auctions. 
As noted above, PJM specifically proposes that for any generation, storage, or 
demand-side resource, “the Accredited UCAP of any BYONC shall be the Accredited 
UCAP for the RPM Auction in which the BYONC cleared for the initial Delivery Year the 
BYONC is in an arrangement with the New Large Load.”20 Accredited UCAP is a defined 
term in the RAA, and denotes the “upper limit on the amount of Unforced Capacity that 
an ELCC Resource can physically provide or offer to provide in the applicable Delivery 
Year.”21 A Tariff provision stating that the “Accredited UCAP” of BYONC will be fixed at 
its initial Delivery Year level indicates that PJM will not account for year-to-year ELCC 
declines in resources supporting BYONC. If the fixed “Accredited UCAP” of BYONC 
offered in an RPM auction exceeds the UCAP that would result from applying updated 
ELCCs to the underlying resources, PJM would be counting (and customers would be 
paying for) megawatts of Accredited UCAP that may not exist. Such a scenario would 
18 Id. at 55-56. Specifically, proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VIII(e) provides that “[a]ll BYONC 
in an arrangement with a New Large Load and not qualifying for an exception pursuant to Tariff, 
Attachment DD, section 6.6(g), must be offered into the applicable RPM Auctions as price takers, i.e., 
$0/MW-day UCAP for a 10-year period starting with the first Delivery Year which the BYONC is in an 
arrangement with the New Large Load.”  
19 See PJM Filing, Transmittal Letter at 56. 
20  PJM Filing, Attachment A, proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VII(i)(i)-(ii) (emphasis added). 
21  PJM Manual 21B, PJM Rules and Procedures for Determination of Generating Capability, Rev. 5 at p. 
21 (effective Jan. 22, 2026). ELCC Resources include Generation Capacity Resources and Demand 
Resources. See RAA, Art. 1 - Definitions.

8 
raise significant reliability and rate reasonableness concerns. Further, it would likely have 
differential impact on the generators that offer capacity into RPM, with some enjoying 
fixed capacity accreditation over time and others facing the risk of variations in ELCC 
values. PJM has not provided a justification for this treatment. 
On the other hand, if resources supporting BYONC will be subject to the usual 
resource accreditation process for each respective BRA over the ten-year must-offer 
period, changes in ELCC over that period could create a divergence between BYONC 
and the New Large Load it is ostensibly supporting. PJM recognizes that New Large 
Loads included in the Variable Resource Requirement Curve should match “the 
corresponding BYONC MW in the supply stack” in order to prevent “artificial price shifts.”22
If the megawatts of BYONC in the RPM auction supply stack are diminished by ELCC 
declines, however, the BYONC will not match the corresponding New Large Loads, 
shifting costs to other customers. 
The PJM Filing does not adequately explain how the proposed treatment of 
BYONC in RPM auctions will produce just and reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory 
outcomes given PJM’s projected ELCC declines for storage and other resources. As with 
the related issues discussed in section II.A above, revisions to PJM’s proposal are 
required to account for the impact of expected ELCC declines in resources supporting 
BYONC.23
22  PJM Filing, Transmittal Letter at 58. 
23  The risks associated with ELCC declines may be mitigated somewhat by PJM’s proposal that BYONC 
resources revert to ordinary Capacity Resources if PJM has sufficient capacity to satisfy the region’s 
Reliability Requirement for three consecutive Delivery Years. See id. at 52 (citing proposed Tariff, 
Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii)). A proviso that New Large Loads and BYONC are essentially “re-
set” after three Delivery Years without a shortfall, however, does not eliminate the concerns in Delivery 
Years where IRAS is operative.

9 
C. 
The Commission should direct PJM to modify its proposal for 
determining Accredited UCAP for BYONC. 
Several solutions were offered during the CIFP process to address concerns about 
declining ELCCs for resources supporting BYONC. One approach would be to re-accredit 
BYONC each year, with penalties if the New Large Load exceeds its supporting BYONC, 
and sell-back rights if the BYONC exceeds the New Large Load. While this would be the 
most accurate approach, PJM argued in the CIFP process that it would add significant 
monitoring and matching requirements to the IRAS framework. 
Another approach would be to set a resource’s Accredited UCAP of BYONC for all 
future Delivery Years using PJM’s preliminary ELCC Class Ratings projection. Under this 
method, PJM would only be required to perform the Accredited UCAP analysis for a 
particular BYONC resource once, but the analysis would reflect projected declines (or 
increases) in ELCC over time. Accordingly, a New Large Load would know up-front 
whether and to what extent it would need to provide for additional BYONC to account for 
ELCC declines in its supporting BYONC resources over time.  
The use of projected ELCC figures to set BYONC Accredited UCAP would, to be 
sure, still result in some level of mismatch between projected and actual ELCC for 
resources supporting BYONC. Given the potential adverse reliability impacts and cost 
shifts associated with resources that have declining accreditations over time, however, it 
is better to err on the side of capturing these projected declines, albeit imprecisely, rather 
than use PJM’s “set and forget” approach to accrediting BYONC. 
PJM’s consent to modifications to the PJM Filing should encompass AMP’s 
proposal to better account for ELCC declines in BYONC resources supporting New Large 
Loads. Such a revision is certainly “consistent with PJM’s overarching objectives in this

10 
filing,”24 inasmuch as it would more precisely encourage New Large Loads “to address 
the capacity shortfall caused by their rapid growth, in both speed to interconnection and 
volume of capacity needed,”25 and better promote “the development of new capacity so 
that the PJM Region has sufficient capacity to maintain reliability without entering into a 
capacity shortage and/or having to shed existing native load customers.”26 These 
revisions would also better reflect PJM’s objective of matching BYONC with 
corresponding New Large Loads to avoid cost shifts in RPM auctions.27 Finally, directing 
PJM to revise its filing to address the discrete concerns identified by AMP would not 
constitute the imposition of an “entirely different rate design” in contravention of NRG.28
III. 
CONCLUSION 
WHEREFORE, for the foregoing reasons, American Municipal Power, Inc. submits 
its limited protest in this proceeding and asks that the Commission consider it in acting 
on the PJM Filing.  
Respectfully submitted,
